vocab: 1. Serfdom
Feudal rule tying unfree peasants to work a lord’s manor without pay.
2. Statute of Labourers
1351 law freezing peasant wages at low pre-plague levels.
3. Poll Tax
Flat tax charging every adult the exact same sum, rich or poor.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: England’s [Demography] changed dramatically after the Black Death of 1348–49 killed over a third of the population and created acute labour shortages. Angry lords passed the 1351 [Statute of Labourers] to freeze wages and preserve [Serfdom]. When King Richard II’s government collected three unfair [Poll Tax] levies by 1381, Wat Tyler and John Ball led a dramatic peasant [Insurrection] into London.

key_individuals.name: King Edward the Confessor
key_individuals.role: Last King of the House of Wessex (1042–1066)
key_individuals.origins: Pious Anglo-Saxon monarch who reigned for twenty-four years and rebuilt Westminster Abbey, yet died childless on 5 January 1066 with no direct blood heir.
key_individuals.significance: His childless death plunged Northwestern Europe into the 1066 succession crisis, leaving the Anglo-Saxon Witan to elect Harold Godwinson while Duke William of Normandy and King Harald Hardrada of Norway prepared rival invasions.
achievements: Allegedly promised the English crown to his cousin Duke William of Normandy in 1051 before naming Earl Harold Godwinson protector of the realm on his deathbed.
Buried in Westminster Abbey in January 1066, within twenty-four hours of which the Witan crowned Harold II.

key_individuals.name: King Harold II (Harold Godwinson)
key_individuals.role: Earl of Wessex & Last Crowned Anglo-Saxon King of England (1066)
key_individuals.origins: England’s wealthiest nobleman and Earl of Wessex, elected king by the Witan in January 1066 despite Norman claims that he had sworn a sacred 1064 oath on holy relics supporting Duke William.
key_individuals.significance: Marched 190 miles north in four days to annihilate Harald Hardrada’s Vikings at Stamford Bridge (25 September 1066), before force-marching 250 miles south to die defending Senlac Hill at Hastings on 14 October 1066.
achievements: Crushed Harald Hardrada’s 300-longship Viking invasion at Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066, leaving only 24 ships needed for the survivors.
Held Senlac Hill near Hastings for five hours behind an interlocking shield wall of elite housecarls and fyrd militia until Norman feigned retreats broke the line and Harold was killed.

key_individuals.name: King Harald Hardrada
key_individuals.role: King of Norway & Viking Claimant to the English Throne (1046–1066)
key_individuals.origins: Fearsome Norwegian warrior-king ("Hard-Ruler") who claimed the English crown through an earlier pact between Scandinavian rulers and sailed 300 Viking longships to Yorkshire in September 1066.
key_individuals.significance: Forced King Harold II to march his elite housecarls 190 miles north just days before Duke William landed at Pevensey—fatally exhausting England’s army even though Hardrada himself was killed at Stamford Bridge.
achievements: Landed 300 Viking longships on the Yorkshire coast in September 1066.
Killed by an arrow to the throat during King Harold’s surprise assault at the Battle of Stamford Bridge (25 September 1066), ending the Viking Age in England.

key_individuals.name: William the Conqueror (Duke William of Normandy)
key_individuals.role: Duke of Normandy & First Norman King of England (1066–1087)
key_individuals.origins: Formidable Duke of Normandy who secured the papal banner of Pope Alexander II, landed unopposed at Pevensey Bay in late September 1066, and defeated Harold II at Hastings using disciplined cavalry feigned retreats.
key_individuals.significance: Subjugated two million Anglo-Saxons with an elite of ten thousand Normans through 500 rapid motte-and-bailey castles, the merciless 1069–70 Harrying of the North, total feudal land redistribution, and the 1086 Domesday Book.
achievements: Won the Battle of Hastings (14 October 1066) by tipping back his helmet to rally panicking troops and ordering feigned cavalry retreats to shatter the Saxon shield wall.
Built over 500 timber motte-and-bailey castles (later stone keeps such as Portchester) and unleashed the Harrying of the North (1069–70), recorded by Orderic Vitalis as starving over 100,000 people.
Commissioned the 1086 Domesday Book survey across every English shire, replacing Anglo-Saxon thegns with ~200 Norman barons bound by feudal knight service.

key_individuals.name: King Henry II
key_individuals.role: First Plantagenet King of England & Ruler of the Angevin Empire (1154–1189)
key_individuals.origins: Energetic Angevin ruler determined to restore royal law and order across England—including ending the scandal of "criminous clerks" escaping royal gallows in lenient Church courts by reading a Latin verse ("benefit of clergy").
key_individuals.significance: Appointed his close friend and Chancellor Thomas Becket as Archbishop of Canterbury in 1162 expecting a loyal ally, issued the 1164 Constitutions of Clarendon, and suffered European outrage and barefoot public penance (1174) after his furious outburst prompted four knights to murder Becket.
achievements: Issued the Constitutions of Clarendon (January 1164) demanding that defrocked criminal clerics face punishment in royal courts.
His angry Christmas 1170 outburst spurred four royal knights to murder Archbishop Becket in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170.
Walked barefoot through Canterbury in July 1174 to be whipped with birch rods by eighty monks at Becket’s shrine, conceding clerical court immunity.

key_individuals.name: Archbishop Thomas Becket
key_individuals.role: Royal Chancellor (1155–62), Archbishop of Canterbury & Canonised Martyr
key_individuals.origins: Once Henry II’s wealthy hunting companion in silk robes, Becket shocked the court upon becoming Archbishop of Canterbury in June 1162 by resigning the Chancellorship, wearing a lice-infested goat hairshirt, and declaring loyalty solely to the Pope.
key_individuals.significance: Refused to seal the 1164 Constitutions of Clarendon, spent six years in French exile, and was hacked down at the altar of Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170—becoming medieval England’s greatest martyr-saint and forcing Henry II to back down over Church courts.
achievements: Defended independent Church courts ("benefit of clergy") against royal jurisdiction at Clarendon (1164) and excommunicated bishops who backed the King in December 1170.
Martyred in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170 and canonised by Pope Alexander III within three years, turning Canterbury into a major European pilgrimage shrine.

key_individuals.name: King John
key_individuals.role: Plantagenet King of England Sealed at Runnymede (1199–1216)
key_individuals.origins: Younger brother of Richard the Lionheart who lost ancestral Normandy to King Philip II of France in 1204 (earning the nickname "John Softsword") and spent a decade squeezing heavy feudal taxes and scutage from English barons.
key_individuals.significance: Provoked a five-year Papal Interdict (1208–13), saw his continental coalition crushed at Bouvines (1214), and—cornered after rebel barons led by Robert Fitzwalter seized London—affixed the Great Seal to Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215.
achievements: Clashed with Pope Innocent III over Archbishop Stephen Langton, enduring the 1208 Interdict and 1209 excommunication before surrendering England as a papal fief in 1213.
Sealed the 63 clauses of Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215—including Clause 39 guaranteeing free men lawful judgement by equals and the law of the land.

Persuaded the Pope to annul Magna Carta within months, sparking the First Barons’ War (and losing crown baggage in the Wash) before dying in October 1216, when William Marshal reissued the Charter for nine-year-old Henry III.

key_individuals.name: Pope Innocent III
key_individuals.role: Head of the Medieval Catholic Church (1198–1216)
key_individuals.origins: Most powerful medieval Pope, who asserted supreme spiritual authority over European monarchs from Rome.
key_individuals.significance: Demonstrated the immense religious power of the medieval papacy by placing all England under a five-year Interdict (1208) and excommunicating King John (1209) until John knelt as a papal vassal—after which Innocent annulled Magna Carta in 1215.
achievements: Locked English church doors for five years under the 1208 Interdict when King John rejected Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury.
Accepted England as a tribute-paying papal fiefdom in 1213, then declared Magna Carta shameful, illegal, and void at John’s request in August 1215.

key_individuals.name: John Ball & Wat Tyler
key_individuals.lifespan: Ball: c. 1338 – July 1381 · Tyler: d. 15 June 1381
key_individuals.role: Radical Preacher & Military Leader of the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt
key_individuals.origins: Following the 1348–50 Black Death, the wage-freezing 1351 Statute of Labourers, and the flat 12-pence third Poll Tax of May 1381 (sparked when Essex villagers chased tax commissioner John Bampton from Brentwood), Kentish rebel Wat Tyler freed radical priest John Ball.
key_individuals.significance: Led over 30,000 Essex and Kent rebels into London in June 1381—burning tax rolls, storming the Tower of London, and preaching human equality ("When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?")—accelerating the long-term collapse of English serfdom.
achievements: John Ball preached radical Christian equality to massed rebels at Blackheath outside London.
Wat Tyler presented demands to abolish serfdom and cap land rents to King Richard II before being stabbed by London’s Mayor at Smithfield on 15 June 1381.

key_individuals.name: King Richard II
key_individuals.role: Fourteen-Year-Old Boy King During the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt (1377–1399)
key_individuals.origins: Fourteen-year-old grandson of Edward III whose royal ministers imposed three regressive Poll Taxes (culminating in 12d per adult in 1381) to pay French war debts from the Hundred Years’ War.
key_individuals.significance: Displayed cool nerve at Mile End and Smithfield on 14–15 June 1381—riding forward when Wat Tyler was killed ("I shall be your captain!") to disperse the rebel army with promises of freedom, before revoking every charter and executing rebel leaders.
achievements: Promised charters abolishing serfdom to disperse armed rebels at Mile End and Smithfield (June 1381).

Revoked his freedom charters once royal forces regrouped ("Villeins ye are, and villeins ye shall remain"), though labour shortages after the Black Death meant feudal bondage steadily withered away anyway.

guided_reading.book_title: Gesta Guillelmi (The Deeds of William): Senlac Hill & the Feigned Retreat
guided_reading.author: William of Poitiers (c. 1071 • Norman Court Chronicle)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Bayeux Tapestry Scene 52 (c. 1070s, Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux): Mail-clad Norman cavalry knights charge uphill against King Harold’s interlocking Anglo-Saxon shield wall at Hastings.
guided_reading.author_context: William of Poitiers (c. 1020–1090) was a Norman chaplain who had trained as a knight before entering the Church and serving Duke William of Normandy. Writing around five years after 1066, his Latin chronicle Gesta Guillelmi flatters his Norman patron, yet provides our most detailed military account of how Norman cavalry broke the English shield-wall on 14 October 1066.
guided_reading.extract:
"The English stood massed tightly upon the crest of the hill, holding the high ground in so dense a wedge that the dead could scarcely fall where they stood. Hurling javelins and wielding terrible two-handed battleaxes that clove through shields and coats of mail alike, King Harold’s warriors drove back our foot-soldiers and Bretons upon the left wing.

When false cries arose among the ranks that Duke William himself had fallen, flight began to spread across the valley. Seeing the peril, the Duke spurred his charger across the path of the retreating knights, pushed back his iron helmet so that every man might behold his bare face, and cried aloud: 'Look at me well! I live, and by God’s grace I shall conquer! What madness drives you to flee when victory lies before you?'

Perceiving thereafter that the tightly locked English shield-wall could not be shattered by headlong assault uphill, the Normans twice turned their horses in deliberate, feigned flight. Drawn down from their ridge in eager pursuit of what seemed a beaten enemy, thousands of the English broke formation on the lower slope—whereupon our horsemen wheeled swiftly round, surrounded the scattered pursuers, and cut them down."

vocabVault.def: A tightly locked defensive formation in which Anglo-Saxon huscarls and fyrdmen overlapped shields on high ground.
Elite, salaried professional bodyguards of the Anglo-Saxon king who fought with heavy mail and two-handed Danish axes.
A disciplined cavalry tactic of pretending to flee in panic in order to lure defenders out of a strong defensive position.
Support and reward given by a powerful ruler to a writer or churchman, often shaping how chronicles praise that ruler.

parent_discussion.question: Why was it almost impossible for Duke William’s soldiers to break the English army during the morning of 14 October 1066?
parent_discussion.answer: Harold’s army held the steep top of Senlac Hill in a tightly locked shield-wall, where Norman horses struggled uphill against two-handed battleaxes.

parent_discussion.question: How did Duke William stop his army panicking when a rumour spread that he had been killed, and how did the feigned retreat work?
parent_discussion.answer: He lifted his helmet to show his face alive, then used pretended retreats to trick English fighters into chasing downhill and breaking their shield-wall.

parent_discussion.question: Knowing that William of Poitiers was Duke William’s own chaplain, why should historians read his praise of Norman cleverness carefully?
parent_discussion.answer: As a Norman court chronicler writing for the Conqueror, he exaggerates William’s genius while downplaying how exhausted Harold’s troops already were after marching south from Stamford Bridge.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: What weapon did the English huscarls use that terrified William’s knights?

Pair: Compare this chronicle with Scene 55 of the Bayeux Tapestry—how do both sources corroborate William lifting his helmet?

Share: Was Hastings won more by Norman tactics or English exhaustion after Stamford Bridge?
questions: Why could the English soldiers on the hilltop "scarcely fall where they stood"?
What did Duke William do with his helmet to prove to his retreating troops that he was still alive?
How did the Norman "feigned flight" trick the English defenders into losing their advantage?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Translated from Latin and condensed for KS3 reading aloud from William of Poitiers’s c. 1071 Norman chronicle.

guided_reading.book_title: Historia Ecclesiastica: Orderic Vitalis on Castles & the Harrying of the North
guided_reading.author: Orderic Vitalis (Book IV, c. 1125 • Monastery of Saint-Évroul)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Bayeux Tapestry Scene 45 (c. 1070s, Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux): Norman overseers force English labourers to dig the steep earthen motte and palisade of Hastings Castle.
guided_reading.author_context: Orderic Vitalis (1075–c. 1142) was born in Shropshire to a Norman father and an English mother before becoming a Benedictine monk in Normandy. Because of his mixed Anglo-Norman heritage, Orderic wrote with rare moral honesty—praising King William’s strength while fiercely condemning the merciless starvation inflicted on Yorkshire during the Harrying of the North (1069–1070).
guided_reading.extract:
"Throughout the conquered shires the King planted royal castles—earthworks crowned with timber palisades that the English had scarcely known before, which prevented the people of the land from rising cleanly against his garrisons. Yet when the men of Northumbria joined Danish raiders at York in 1069, King William’s wrath knew no restraint.

Nowhere else had William shown such cruelty. Yielding to his anger, he spared neither the weak nor the innocent, commanding that all crops, herds of cattle, ploughs, and stores of grain between York and Durham be burned to ashes so that rebels might find no winter sustenance.

From that deliberate ruin so dreadful a famine swept across northern England that defenceless men, women, and children perished of hunger upon the frozen roads—more than one hundred thousand Christian souls, as men reckoned. Though I have often praised King William’s vigour and order, I dare not excuse so brutal a slaughter; for surely Almighty God, the righteous Judge, will weigh the cries of the starving alongside the deeds of princes."

vocabVault.def: A Norman fortress combining a raised earthen mound (motte) topped by a wooden keep with a fenced courtyard (bailey) below.
Systematic scorched-earth devastation—burning crops, livestock, and villages to starve a region into submission.
A body of armed knights and soldiers stationed inside a castle to control the surrounding countryside.
Bringing a conquered population completely under royal obedience through force, law, and taxation.

parent_discussion.question: Why were Norman motte-and-bailey castles such a shock and threat to Anglo-Saxon communities?
parent_discussion.answer: England had very few private castles before 1066; towering earthen mottes and mounted garrisons allowed small numbers of Normans to dominate whole shires.

parent_discussion.question: Why did King William burn ploughs, barns, and cattle across Yorkshire in the winter of 1069–1070 rather than simply fighting rebel soldiers?
parent_discussion.answer: By destroying food supplies and tools ("scorched earth"), he ensured no northern rebellion or Danish army could feed itself—causing catastrophic famine for civilians.

parent_discussion.question: Why does Orderic Vitalis’s mixed English and Norman background make his verdict on William so valuable to historians?
parent_discussion.answer: Even though he lived in a Norman monastery and admired William’s order, his English roots made him refuse to whitewash the starvation of innocent northern families.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: What triggered William’s fury in northern England in 1069?

Pair: Note Orderic’s figure of "100,000" dead—why did medieval chroniclers use huge round numbers, and how does the 1086 Domesday Book ("wasteland" / vasta) prove the devastation really happened?

Share: Which did more to secure Norman control permanently: castles, terror, or Domesday taxation?
questions: What new type of fortification did King William build across the English shires?
What items did William order his troops to burn between York and Durham in 1069–1070?
Why does Orderic Vitalis say he "dare not excuse" William’s actions in the North?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Translated from Latin and condensed for KS3 pupils from Orderic Vitalis’s c. 1125 monastic chronicle.

guided_reading.book_title: Vita Sancti Thomae: Eyewitness Account of the Murder in the Cathedral
guided_reading.author: Edward Grim (c. 1172 • British Library Cotton MS Claudius B II)
guided_reading.cover_caption: British Library Harley MS 5102, f. 32 (c. 1220): Eyewitness clerk Edward Grim holds the cross at the altar as four Norman knights murder Archbishop Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170.
guided_reading.author_context: Edward Grim was a clerk from Cambridge visiting Archbishop Thomas Becket at Canterbury on the evening of 29 December 1170. When four household knights of King Henry II—Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, and Richard le Breton—stormed into the cathedral, Grim stood beside Becket and had his own arm nearly severed by the first sword blow before writing this famous eyewitness biography.
guided_reading.extract:
"As twilight fell on the twenty-ninth of December, the monks hurried Archbishop Thomas toward the cathedral vespers, begging him to bolt the heavy oak doors behind them. Turning calmly upon the steps, Thomas forbade them: 'It is not right to turn the fortress of prayer, the Church of Christ, into a military camp. Even if it stands unlocked, it is able to shield its own; we shall triumph over our foes by suffering rather than by fighting.'

Moments later the four mailed knights burst in with drawn swords and axes, shouting aloud: 'Where is Thomas Becket, traitor to the King and the realm?' Receiving no answer, they cried again, 'Where is the Archbishop?' At once Thomas stepped down from the pillar into plain view and answered clearly: 'Here I am—no traitor to the King, but a priest of God. What do you seek?'

When they demanded that he lift the excommunication placed upon the King’s bishops, Thomas refused unless they submitted to the authority of the Church. Though I threw my own arm forward to turn aside the first descending blade—whereby my arm was grievously cut—the Archbishop bowed his head in prayer, commending his cause to God and St Denis, and fell beneath their swords upon the stone pavement."

vocabVault.def: The most senior churchman in England, responsible for leading the English Church under the Pope in Rome.
Officially expelling a person from the Catholic Church and its sacraments—a terrifying spiritual punishment in medieval Europe.
A person killed because they refuse to surrender their religious faith or principles.
A public act of sorrow and punishment carried out to seek God’s forgiveness for a grave sin.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Archbishop Thomas Becket refuse to let the terrified monks lock the doors of Canterbury Cathedral?
parent_discussion.answer: He insisted a church is a house of prayer, not a castle, believing sacred sanctuary should never be barred to anyone.

parent_discussion.question: What was the core argument between King Henry II and Becket that led the four knights to confront him?
parent_discussion.answer: Who held supreme authority over Church courts and bishops in England—the Crown (Constitutions of Clarendon) or the Church and Pope.

parent_discussion.question: How did murdering Becket inside Canterbury Cathedral completely backfire on King Henry II?
parent_discussion.answer: Christendom was horrified; Becket was swiftly declared a saint and martyr, forcing Henry II to walk barefoot through Canterbury to be whipped in penance in 1174 and compromise on Church courts.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Why is Edward Grim such an extraordinary eyewitness source for 29 December 1170?

Pair: At the same time, Grim wrote to celebrate Becket as a saint—which details in his account emphasize Becket’s saintly bravery?

Share: Who won the struggle between Crown and Church after 1170: Henry II or Becket?

guided_reading.book_title: Flores Historiarum & Magna Carta: Confrontation at Runnymede (June 1215)
guided_reading.author: Roger of Wendover (St Albans Chronicle, c. 1235) & Magna Carta Clauses 12, 39 & 61
guided_reading.cover_caption: James William Edmund Doyle, John Signs the Great Charter (1864): King John confronted by armed rebel barons and Archbishop Stephen Langton in the meadow of Runnymede on 15 June 1215.
guided_reading.author_context: Roger of Wendover (died 1236) was the chronicler of St Albans Abbey, a great monastery just north of London through which royal officials and rebel barons constantly passed. Paired here with the translated Latin text of the Great Charter sealed at Runnymede on 15 June 1215, his account captures how military defeat in France and crushing scutage taxes forced King John to accept the rule of law.
guided_reading.extract:
Roger of Wendover records how England’s barons renounced their fealty in the spring of 1215 after years of arbitrary fines, lost wars in Normandy, and heavy scutage taxes: "Gathering an army styling itself the Army of God and Holy Church, the barons marched upon London, whose citizens opened the city gates to them. Seeing himself deserted by almost all his knights save a handful of foreign mercenaries, King John met the barons in the water-meadow called Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines, on the fifteenth day of June."

There the King’s Great Seal was pressed into wax beneath the clauses of Magna Carta:
"Clause 12: No scutage or aid shall be imposed in our kingdom unless by the common counsel of our kingdom..."
"Clause 39: No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, nor will we proceed with force against him, except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land."
"Clause 40: To no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice."
"Clause 61: The barons shall choose any twenty-five barons of the kingdom to observe, hold, and cause to be observed the peace and liberties which we have granted."

vocabVault.def: "Shield money"—a feudal tax demanded by King John instead of military service, which he levied eleven times to fund failed wars.
In 1215, landowners, knights, barons, and townsmen who were not unfree peasant villeins tied to a lord’s manor.
The constitutional principle that even the monarch must obey the law rather than ruling by personal whim.
The water-meadow beside the River Thames near Windsor where King John agreed to Magna Carta on 15 June 1215.

parent_discussion.question: Why had England’s barons grown furious enough with King John to capture London in 1215?
parent_discussion.answer: John had lost Normandy to France, demanded repeated scutage taxes, seized barons’ castles and hostages without trial, and quarrelled with the Pope.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Clauses 39 and 40 not immediately give rights to everyone living in England in 1215?
parent_discussion.answer: Clause 39 applied only to "free men" (barons, knights, and freemen), leaving out the majority of English peasants who were unfree villeins.

parent_discussion.question: Even if the barons in 1215 mainly wanted to protect their own wealth (plus Clause 61’s committee of 25 barons), why did Magna Carta become world-famous?
parent_discussion.answer: It established in writing that the king is beneath the law, cannot imprison people without fair trial, and cannot tax the realm without common consent.

guided_reading.hinge_question:

Pair: Look closely at Clause 39 and Clause 61: which clause lasted for 800 years, and which clause caused civil war within months?

Share: Was Magna Carta a timeless charter of human liberty or a feudal barons’ power grab?

guided_reading.book_title: Historia Anglicana: John Ball’s Blackheath Sermon & the 1381 Rising
guided_reading.author: Thomas Walsingham (St Albans Abbey Chronicle, c. 1381–1394)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Jean Froissart, Chroniques (c. 1470–1475, British Library Royal MS 18 E I, f. 165v): Radical priest John Ball ('Jehan Balle') preaching equality to Wat Tyler ('Waultre le Tieulier') and the rebel host at Blackheath in June 1381.
guided_reading.author_context: After the Black Death (1348–1349) killed between a third and half of England’s population, surviving peasants realised their labour was scarce—yet lords enforced the 1351 Statute of Labourers to freeze wages and imposed three flat-rate Poll Taxes between 1377 and 1381. Monastic chronicler Thomas Walsingham of St Albans disliked the rebels intensely, yet preserved the revolutionary words preached by radical priest John Ball at Blackheath on 12 June 1381.
guided_reading.extract:
"After the Commons of Kent and Essex had broken open Maidstone gaol and freed the priest John Ball, a vast multitude of country folk gathered upon Blackheath overlooking London. Taking for his text the rhyme that had passed secretly from village to village, John Ball preached thus to the throng:

'When Adam delved [dug] and Eve span [spun wool], who was then the gentleman? From the beginning all human beings were created equal by nature; bondage and serfdom were brought in not by God’s will, but by the unjust oppression of wicked men! Now is the hour given to you by God, if you have the courage, to cast off the heavy yoke of villeinage that you have borne so long, and win the liberty you have always desired.'

Stirred by his words and enraged by the collectors of the third Poll Tax, the rebels marched under Wat Tyler across London Bridge, burned the legal manor rolls that recorded their unfree birth, and demanded of fourteen-year-old King Richard II at Mile End that no man in England should henceforth be a serf."

vocabVault.def: Unfree feudal status tying peasants to their lord’s manor, requiring unpaid week-work and fines for permission to marry or move.
The hated flat-rate "head tax" of 1381 in which a poor farm labourer had to pay the exact same twelve pence (three groats) as a wealthy lord.
Written parchment court records held by lords that proved which families owed unfree feudal labour.
The medieval hierarchy exchanging land for loyalty, knight-service, and peasant labour.

parent_discussion.question: What did John Ball mean by his famous question, "When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?"
parent_discussion.answer: In the biblical Garden of Eden there were no lords or serfs—so class inequality and serfdom were invented by human greed, not ordained by God.

parent_discussion.question: How were the Black Death of 1348 and the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 directly connected?
parent_discussion.answer: The plague created a severe shortage of workers; when Parliament blocked rising wages (1351 Statute of Labourers) and added unfair Poll Taxes, emboldened peasants rebelled.

parent_discussion.question: Why did the rebels in 1381 deliberately target and burn parchment manor rolls rather than looting randomly?
parent_discussion.answer: Burning the written legal records of villeinage showed they had clear political goals: erasing proof of unfree serfdom so they could rent land freely for cash wages.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Why was the 1381 Poll Tax considered far more unfair than normal taxes?

Pair: Thomas Walsingham was a wealthy abbey chronicler whose own monastery owned serfs—how might that bias his attitude toward Wat Tyler and John Ball?

Share: Even though Wat Tyler and John Ball were killed in 1381, why had serfdom largely disappeared across England within seventy years?
